candidate.blueprint_topic: Medication indication, response evaluation, and coagulation-laboratory interpretation
candidate.educational_objective: Interpret an incomplete INR response to phytonadione in cirrhosis by distinguishing correctable vitamin K deficiency from liver-related synthetic dysfunction and by recognizing that INR alone does not reliably quantify bleeding risk in cirrhosis.

options.A: Persistent INR elevation may reflect liver-related impairment of clotting-factor synthesis rather than correctable vitamin K deficiency; repeated large phytonadione doses are not warranted simply because the INR remains high.
options.B: Any prolonged INR in cirrhosis proves vitamin K deficiency, so phytonadione should be repeated until the INR reaches a universal normal target.
options.C: A prolonged INR in cirrhosis directly quantifies bleeding risk, so failure to normalize it means major bleeding is inevitable.
options.D: Phytonadione is contraindicated whenever chronic liver disease is present, even when a true vitamin K deficiency is contributing.

candidate.rationale: A is correct. Phytonadione is indicated when hypoprothrombinemia is caused by vitamin K deficiency or interference with vitamin K activity. Current DailyMed labeling specifically states that repeated large doses are not warranted in liver disease if the initial response is unsatisfactory and that failure to respond may indicate a condition inherently unresponsive to phytonadione. AASLD explains that prolonged PT/INR is common in liver dysfunction because liver-derived coagulation factors are reduced, but INR measures only procoagulant factors and does not account for simultaneous reductions in anticoagulant factors. Therefore, INR alone is not a reliable measure of bleeding risk in cirrhosis and there is no universal target INR for routine correction. B incorrectly assumes every elevated INR is vitamin K deficiency and invents a universal correction target. C overstates INR as a direct bleeding-risk measure. D is incorrect because phytonadione can be appropriate when genuine vitamin K deficiency or interference is present; chronic liver disease itself is not a blanket contraindication.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Phytonadione is appropriate for vitamin K-deficiency/interference states, but an unsatisfactory response in liver disease does not justify repeated large doses. In cirrhosis, INR prolongation can reflect impaired hepatic synthesis and INR alone is not a reliable bleeding-risk measure or a universal target for correction.
